My name is Hoot. One thing about me is that I am always listening. I hear the rustle of leaves, the scurrying of mice, the distant call of a barn owl. I listen for the night, and when I hear something, I fly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My name is Hoot. I am the owl who lives in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. I have been here for many seasons, and the wood is my home. I am a tawny owl, with brown feathers and yellow eyes. I hunt at night, and I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to my mate, who answers "chee-wee." I have two young this year, and I watch over them from the branches.

I drink from the stream that runs through the meadow. I sit on the bank and let the water run over my beak. It's cool and clean, and it helps me stay hydrated. I also drink from the dew on the leaves in the morning. I don't need much, but I always make sure I have water nearby. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Water is far away. I hear it as a distant, soft, rushing sound, like the wind through the reeds. It's not loud, but it's constant. Sometimes I think it's the stream near the meadow, but I don't go there. I know it's there, though. I've heard it all my life. It's the sound of the world moving, even when I'm still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. The one that runs through the meadow behind the wood. I can hear it from my tree, and I can see it from the top of the oak. It's where the voles go to drink, and where the water shrews come out at dusk. I've seen a heron stand on it once, still as a log. I don't like the heron. It takes the voles.

It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the wind moves the grass and the voles run. The stream is a boundary, and I do not cross it. The meadow is dark in the dusk, and the voles are quick. I hear them under the leaves. I call, and they run. I wait. I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not go there often, for it is too open and the owls are fewer. But sometimes, when the moon is full, I fly over the meadow to the stream. The water is cold, and the fish are silver. Grassy places are where the voles are. The meadow beyond the stream, the field where the farmer mows in the summer, the bankside where the rabbits come to drink. I hunt there in the dark, with the wind in my feathers and the moon in my eyes. I hear the rustle of a vole in the grass, I drop, and the grass is still.

Mice. The ones that run in the meadow. I hear them in the dark, and I strike. I eat them whole, bones and all. The voles are good too, but they are more cautious. I catch them in the wood. The shrews are small and quick, but I can still catch them. The moths are a treat, but they are not enough. I need more. I need the mice.

I do not have a favourite prey. I eat what I find, when I find it. Mice are common, and they are good. Voles are fat and slow, but they are not always easy to catch. Moths are quick, but they are not always enough. I eat what I need, and I do not choose. I am a hunter, not a chooser. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I sit still and wait. When I hear a rustle, I fly down and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I find a mouse or a shrew. The long grass is good cover. I don't like the open fields. They are too noisy.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry, and the bark is rough. I have a nest of twigs and leaves. I sleep there at night, and I watch the meadow from the top. The wind sometimes howls through the branches, and I hoot to show I am there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a good view of the meadow and the lane. I sleep in the back of it, where the branches are thick. I have a nest of twigs and leaves, and I keep it clean. The wind sometimes makes it creak, but I like the sound. I am safe here, and I am not alone.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and the bark is rough. I have nested there for three years. The stream is below, and the meadow is beyond. I can hear the meadow from the hollow, and the wind through the trees. I have a mate who calls from the other side of the stream, and we have a brood of young. I am Hoot. I am home.
